name: Nicaragua
summary_text: Nicaragua does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or trans identity. Article 204 of the Criminal Code, inserted by religious legislators into a bill originally drafted to protect women from rape and signed into law in July 1992, made it an offence punishable by up to three years' imprisonment to "induce, promote, propagandize, or practice sex among persons of the same sex in a scandalous manner"; the Supreme Court rejected an unconstitutionality challenge in March 1994. The provision's vagueness had also made it usable against LGBT-rights organising and sexual-health work. Its language was dropped when a new Penal Code took effect on 1 March 2008, and same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since.  Formal legality does not translate into protection. The US State Department's 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices in Nicaragua documents a police and parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against perceived opponents of the government that authorities did not investigate or prosecute, and lists violence or threats against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex persons among the year's significant human rights violations. The official US assessment places anti-LGBTI abuse inside a broader climate of state impunity.  Amnesty International's May 2019 reporting places homophobia inside that same repression. The crackdown on protests that began in April 2018 left at least 325 people dead and more than 2,000 injured, according to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, and journalist Miguel Mora described being beaten by a pro-government mob and being targeted partly for being gay.  Documented violence against LGBT people is persistent and under-recorded. A 2012 Center for Justice and International Law survey counted 53 aggressions between 1999 and 2011, among them 15 murders: 10 gay men, 4 transgender people and 1 lesbian, with the true total expected to be higher. The NGO Programa Feminista La Corriente reported 67 assaults, 1 hate crime or murder and 2 suicides in 2021; 39 assaults, 3 hate crimes and 1 suicide in 2022; 35 assaults, 2 hate crimes, 1 murder, 1 suicide, 2 sexual assaults and 1 extortion in 2023; and 13 assaults, 5 hate crimes and 1 missing person in the first two quarters of 2024. Trans women are the most targeted group, and state police are among the aggressors, tied with family members in 2022. Attacks go largely unreported out of fear of retaliation and poor legal outcomes.  Family-law exclusion is explicit. The Family Code approved by the Nicaraguan Congress in June 2014, in force from 8 April 2015, limits marriage, partnerships and adoption to heterosexual couples, and Article 72 of the Constitution defines marriage and stable unions as resting on voluntary agreement between a man and a woman. Same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal benefits and protections available to opposite-sex married couples. Several organisations filed an action of unconstitutionality against the Code. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 holds that parties to the American Convention on Human Rights must grant same-sex couples access to all domestic family-registration rights including marriage, and no Nicaraguan implementation is recorded.  Discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds is barred in several settings, including health care. Ministerial Resolution 671-2014 bars discrimination in access to health services on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, which is the provision most directly relevant to a visitor seeking care.  Public opinion is largely opposed. A Pew survey conducted from 9 November to 13 December 2013 found 77% opposed to same-sex marriage, 16% in favour and 7% unsure, while the 2017 AmericasBarometer showed 24.5% support.

name: Netherlands
summary_text: Visa requirements for the Netherlands depend on nationality alone. Transgender and non-binary visitors are not treated differently in visa applications, and a passport carrying a gender marker other than the one assigned at birth, or an 'X' marker, is accepted for entry provided it was officially issued. No additional gender documentation may be demanded at the border.  Discrimination on grounds of gender identity is prohibited. Gender expression became an explicitly protected ground under the Equal Treatment Act in March 2019, following passage by the House of Representatives in 2018 (127 votes to 23) and the Senate on 12 March 2019 (64 to 11), after the Netherlands Institute for Human Rights had already treated transgender people as covered by the word 'gender' in earlier cases. Since February 2023, sexual orientation and disability are formally written into Article 1 of the Constitution.  Since 1 July 2025, a discriminatory motive is codified in Dutch law as a ground for increasing penalties in criminal cases, operating alongside expanded victims' rights and protection of victim data. Dutch legislation nonetheless contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime'; police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through the police Centre of Expertise Discrimination (ECAD-P), which is the framework behind published hate-crime statistics.  Reported anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination is rising. Police recorded 4,800 discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people last year, up 7.5% on 2024 and up 81% from 2,654 in 2022, with reports concerning transgender people up 51% in a year (264 to 399). The COC described the figures as extremely worrying and noted only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination in the same year. Official Dutch government figures state that over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence, including 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people, and that incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence rose sharply per the 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism; in 2022, one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation.  During WorldPride Amsterdam 2026, more than 70 people reported discrimination through the RITA platform in the opening period, mostly festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and Pride Walk participants; RITA warned the reports are only a fraction of the total. Amsterdam broadened 'Safer Spaces' reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence during World Pride to cover the Nieuwe Kerk, the Stedelijk Museum, the Stadsarchief, hotels and a central RITA location, with 1.4 million visitors expected. Mayor Femke Halsema told the council that Amsterdam will tackle discrimination and violent incidents with priority during World Pride, with police, enforcer and organiser agreements to act fast; recent Prides drew 25 to 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene.  Legal gender change in the Netherlands still requires a medical expert letter, falling short of self-determination. The 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure taking three to nine months, and the Transgender Act (self-ID) was withdrawn in July 2025. Compensation was offered to people sterilised under earlier rules. Legal gender recognition has otherwise been administrative since a December 2013 law took effect in 2014, removing the earlier requirement of surgery and sterilisation imposed by the 1984-85 laws.  Transgender detainees occupy an unregulated space in Dutch law. No law, regulation or official policy governs their placement: the Penitentiary Principles Act only separates male and female detainees, and the Prison Service (DJI) confirmed placement is based on the gender designation in the municipal records (BRP) together with case-by-case factors such as gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background, and physical or mental health. The Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights (NJCM) advised the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection, Robine van der Meer and later Minister Weerwind, in a letter of 21 February 2024 that this absence of rules is worrying and undesirable, noting international research documenting human-rights violations including discrimination and sexual violence against transgender detainees, the absence of official figures on the number of transgender detainees, and the relevance of CPT standards. Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an 'Extra Care Facility' (EZV) wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they sit alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. Documented cases include a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing before transfer to an EZV; a parole-board appeals ruling of 21 March 2016 (15/4323/GB) concerning a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation; and rulings by the Limburg court (17 October 2017, ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624) and The Hague appeals court (29 June 2020, ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108) treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. NJCM asked the minister to create CPT-aligned rules placing transgender detainees by gender identity; the DIZ said it was drafting guidelines, unpublished at the time.  Access to care: Dutch insurance fully covers PrPreP and related care for gay and bisexual men from 1 August 2019 at all Municipal Health Services (GGD) offices. Assisted insemination for infertility is covered by health insurance regardless of whether the patient is single, in an opposite-sex couple or a lesbian couple. The 2016 Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport guidelines, endorsed by eight medical organisations including the Dutch Psychiatry Association and Transvisie, recommend puberty blockers for transgender adolescents at Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, and top surgery is available to patients over 16. In July 2026 the Dutch Health Board reaffirmed gender-affirming care for trans youth, citing harms of delay, mental-health improvements and a low regret rate. Conversion therapy has been excluded from health insurance coverage since June 2012 and the practice was banned by a bill ratified on 8 September 2026.  Open military service has been permitted for gay people since homosexuality's declassification as a mental illness in 1973 and for transgender people as well. Equaldex records the Netherlands as recognising non-binary gender, protecting bathroom access, and prohibiting discrimination in employment and housing on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds, while noting that hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only. The Netherlands ranks 13th on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026.

sources.title: Equal Treatment Act 1994 (Algemene wet gelijke behandeling)
sources.documents: Bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in employment, housing, public/private accommodations; extended in 2019 to explicitly include gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics; 'single fact' loophole for religious schools removed.
sources.detail: Enacted March 1994; extension bill introduced 16 Jan 2017, House 3 July 2018 (127-23), Senate 12 March 2019 (64-11); single-fact removal House 27 May 2014 (141-9), Senate 10 March 2015 (72-3), effective 1 July 2015

In July 2026 the Dutch Health Board reaffirmed gender-affirming care for trans youth, citing harms of delay, mental-health improvements and a low regret rate. Conversion therapy has been excluded from health insurance coverage since June 2012 and the practice was banned by a bill ratified on 8 September 2026.  Open military service has been permitted for gay people since homosexuality's declassification as a mental illness in 1973 and for transgender people as well. Equaldex records the Netherlands as recognising non-binary gender, protecting bathroom access, and prohibiting discrimination in employment and housing on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds, while noting that hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only. The Netherlands ranks 13th on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026.

name: Netherlands
summary_text: Visa requirements for the Netherlands depend on nationality alone. Transgender and non-binary visitors are not treated differently in visa applications, and a passport carrying a gender marker other than the one assigned at birth, or an 'X' marker, is accepted for entry provided it was officially issued. No additional gender documentation may be demanded at the border.  Discrimination on grounds of gender identity is prohibited. Gender expression became an explicitly protected ground under the Equal Treatment Act in March 2019, following passage by the House of Representatives in 2018 (127 votes to 23) and the Senate on 12 March 2019 (64 to 11), after the Netherlands Institute for Human Rights had already treated transgender people as covered by the word 'gender' in earlier cases. Since February 2023, sexual orientation and disability are formally written into Article 1 of the Constitution.  Since 1 July 2025, a discriminatory motive is codified in Dutch law as a ground for increasing penalties in criminal cases, operating alongside expanded victims' rights and protection of victim data. Dutch legislation nonetheless contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime'; police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through the police Centre of Expertise Discrimination (ECAD-P), which is the framework behind published hate-crime statistics.  Reported anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination is rising. Police recorded 4,800 discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people last year, up 7.5% on 2024 and up 81% from 2,654 in 2022, with reports concerning transgender people up 51% in a year (264 to 399). The COC described the figures as extremely worrying and noted only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination in the same year. Official Dutch government figures state that over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence, including 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people, and that incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence rose sharply per the 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism; in 2022, one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation.  During WorldPride Amsterdam 2026, more than 70 people reported discrimination through the RITA platform in the opening period, mostly festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and Pride Walk participants; RITA warned the reports are only a fraction of the total. Amsterdam broadened 'Safer Spaces' reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence during World Pride to cover the Nieuwe Kerk, the Stedelijk Museum, the Stadsarchief, hotels and a central RITA location, with 1.4 million visitors expected. Mayor Femke Halsema told the council that Amsterdam will tackle discrimination and violent incidents with priority during World Pride, with police, enforcer and organiser agreements to act fast; recent Prides drew 25 to 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene.  Legal gender change in the Netherlands still requires a medical expert letter, falling short of self-determination. The 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure taking three to nine months, and the Transgender Act (self-ID) was withdrawn in July 2025. Compensation was offered to people sterilised under earlier rules. Legal gender recognition has otherwise been administrative since a December 2013 law took effect in 2014, removing the earlier requirement of surgery and sterilisation imposed by the 1984-85 laws.  Transgender detainees occupy an unregulated space in Dutch law. No law, regulation or official policy governs their placement: the Penitentiary Principles Act only separates male and female detainees, and the Prison Service (DJI) confirmed placement is based on the gender designation in the municipal records (BRP) together with case-by-case factors such as gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background, and physical or mental health. The Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights (NJCM) advised the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection, Robine van der Meer and later Minister Weerwind, in a letter of 21 February 2024 that this absence of rules is worrying and undesirable, noting international research documenting human-rights violations including discrimination and sexual violence against transgender detainees, the absence of official figures on the number of transgender detainees, and the relevance of CPT standards. Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an 'Extra Care Facility' (EZV) wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they sit alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. Documented cases include a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing before transfer to an EZV; a parole-board appeals ruling of 21 March 2016 (15/4323/GB) concerning a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation; and rulings by the Limburg court (17 October 2017, ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624) and The Hague appeals court (29 June 2020, ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108) treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. NJCM asked the minister to create CPT-aligned rules placing transgender detainees by gender identity; the DIZ said it was drafting guidelines, unpublished at the time.  Access to care: Dutch insurance fully covers PrPreP and related care for gay and bisexual men from 1 August 2019 at all Municipal Health Services (GGD) offices. Assisted insemination for infertility is covered by health insurance regardless of whether the patient is single, in an opposite-sex couple or a lesbian couple. The 2016 Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport guidelines, endorsed by eight medical organisations including the Dutch Psychiatry Association and Transvisie, recommend puberty blockers for transgender adolescents at Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, and top surgery is available to patients over 16. In July 2026 the Dutch Health Board reaffirmed gender-affirming care for trans youth, citing harms of delay, mental-health improvements and a low regret rate. Conversion therapy has been excluded from health insurance coverage since June 2012 and the practice was banned by a bill ratified on 8 September 2026.  Open military service has been permitted for gay people since homosexuality's declassification as a mental illness in 1973 and for transgender people as well. The Netherlands ranks 13th on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026.

sources.documents: Documents prior law (voted 1984-1985, in force 1985-2014) requiring gender-affirming surgery and forced sterilization to change legal gender; state apology and €5,000 compensation per victim.
